title: News vs noise
desc: Priced in: why good news can still sink a price

cards.title: Big news, small move
cards.situation: Traders had expected a rate cut for weeks. Today it came. Stocks rose just 0.1%. Why so little?

options.feedback: The news hit every screen in seconds. Traders had already bought on the expectation.
Prices already reflected the cut. With no surprise, there was little left to move.

options.text: Rate cuts are bad for stocks
options.feedback: Cuts usually help stocks. The move was small because traders had expected this cut for weeks.

cards.work: Expected cut 0.25 points. Actual cut 0.25 points. Surprise: zero.

cards.title: Headlines move prices, briefly
cards.text: Most headlines cause a quick jump that fades. Ask one question first: **is this already [[priced-in|priced in]]?**

visual.title: Headline day
visual.label: A stock jumps 3% on a headline at 10:00, then fades to +0.4% at the close

blocks.tip: If everyone expected it, the price has likely moved already.

cards.title: Good news, falling price
cards.text: Prices move on the news versus what was expected. Same profit growth, three outcomes.

visual.label: Same +20% profit growth against three expectations

rows.note: Beat by 10 points: a happy surprise.
Just as expected: nothing new to price in.
Missed by 10 points: good, but not good enough.

cards.foot: Good news can still sink a price if it’s less good than hoped.

cards.title: Rico’s headline filter
cards.text: Before you trade a headline, ask three questions. Not **yes** to all three? Let it pass.

items.title: Is it a surprise versus what was expected?
Does it change the next year, not just today?

cards.title: Beat or miss?
cards.q: A company reports profit up 15%. Analysts expected 25%. The stock falls 8%. Why?

options.feedback: Profit grew, but less than hoped. The price had been set for 25%.
Profit grew, but 10 points less than hoped. The price had been set for 25%.

options.text: Traders hadn’t read the report yet
options.feedback: The report hits screens in seconds. Traders sold because profit grew less than the 25% they expected.
Nothing says the market crashed. This stock fell because profit grew less than the 25% expected.

cards.title: Phone buzzing
cards.q: Ten headlines about the economy hit your phone today. What’s the best approach for a beginner?

options.text: Trade each one fast, before others do
options.feedback: Chasing every headline means paying spreads and getting bounced in and out. Most news is noise.

options.text: Act only on news that’s new, surprising and lasting
options.feedback: News that’s new, surprising and lasting can change the outlook. Most of the rest is noise you can let pass.

options.text: Do the opposite of every headline
options.feedback: Doing the opposite is still trading every headline. Most news is noise: filter it first.

options.text: Turn off your stops for the day
options.feedback: Stops matter most on busy news days, when price can jump. Keep them on.

cards.headline: You can tell news from noise.
lines: Headlines often move prices only briefly.
Ask: is it new, a surprise, or already priced in?
Most days, the best trade on a headline is none.
